tour.title: Hanok Village: Courtyards, Bibimbap & Makgeolli
tour.summary: A winter day through Korea's only city-centre hanok quarter — a king's portrait, a Confucian school, a cathedral built on an execution ground, the market that fed the city, and a makgeolli lane to end it.
tour.overviewText:
Jeonju in the last week of December smells of boiling soybean sprouts and wet stone. Steam rolls out of the market doorways, the tiled roofs go grey-blue with cold, and the courtyards are the only warm places to stand outdoors. This is the right season for this city, because Jeonju is the place Koreans come to eat.

Why Jeonju matters starts with a family. It was the ancestral home of the Yi clan, and in 1392 a Yi — the general Yi Seong-gye — overthrew the Goryeo dynasty and founded Joseon, which ruled Korea until 1910. He was born far to the north-east, but the new dynasty named Jeonju pungpae-jihyang, "the hometown of the founding king", and in 1410 built a shrine here to hold his portrait. Jeonju had mattered long before that: in 900 it was the capital of Later Baekje, one of the three states of the Later Three Kingdoms period. It kept mattering because of the ground: the Honam plain is Korea's rice basket, so Jeonju became a market town and eventually a city that argues about food the way other cities argue about football. UNESCO made it Korea's first Creative City of Gastronomy in 2012.

The political layers are visible on foot. In 1894 the Donghak Peasant Revolution — a peasant army rising against a corrupt court and foreign interference — occupied Jeonju and forced the government into a truce signed here. Japan used that crisis to send troops, and by 1910 Korea was a colony. Under colonial rule Japanese businesses took the flat downtown, the city wall came down in 1911 leaving only its south gate, and Korean families answered by building their own houses on the slope behind the shrine: thick-timbered, tile-roofed, deliberately Korean. That is why this village is not medieval — the oldest houses here are barely a century old.

Religion sits on the same few streets. A Confucian provincial school, where officials were trained in the ancestor rites that held the state together, stands above the lanes. Two hundred metres away, a red-brick cathedral was raised on the ground where Catholics were executed in 1791 for refusing those same rites. Two systems, one argument, one short walk.

The route is straightforward. Start at the shrine on the western edge of the village and work east and uphill through the lanes; come back down past the church and the last of the old city gates to the market, then finish with a taxi ride south to the makgeolli houses. Allow a full day: the closing hours and the light both reward this order.

Practicals: late December runs about 3 to 4°C by day and three to five below freezing at night; it is the driest month, and the light dies around 17:30, so start by 09:30. Gyeonggijeon closes at 18:00 with the last ticket at 17:00; the Confucian school and the market's youth floor both shut Mondays; and the market's night market runs only on Fridays and Saturdays — 29 and 30 December 2026 are a Tuesday and a Wednesday, so plan that evening around the makgeolli houses. Prices are in won (₩); everything moves, so verify every fee and hour at the gate.

Eat slowly. You are in the one Korean city where that is the main event.
tour.difficulty: Easy walking with one stiff climb. Lanes are flat but uneven, with cobbles, raised thresholds and a stone staircase up Omokdae that ices over in winter. The final leg south to the makgeolli lane is long and better ridden than walked.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at opening time, around 09:30, so you clear Gyeonggijeon and the Confucian school before their winter closings and reach Omokdae in the low early-afternoon light, when the rooftops read best. Finish in the market for a late lunch, then take a taxi to the makgeolli houses for an early dinner — most close around 22:00.

stops.name: Gyeonggijeon Shrine
stops.narration:
This walled compound holds the face of the man who founded Korea's longest-lived dynasty. Gyeonggijeon was built in 1410, in the tenth year of King Taejong, to enshrine the portrait of King Taejo — born Yi Seong-gye — a general who overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and became the first king of Joseon, which then ruled the peninsula until 1910. Taejo was born far to the north-east, but his clan, the Jeonju Yi, came from here, so the dynasty declared Jeonju pungpae-jihyang, "the hometown of the founding king", and gave it a portrait hall. Portraits of Taejo were once enshrined in six places across the country; this is the only one that survived.

What hangs in the hall is an 1872 copy, National Treasure No. 317, painted by the court's best hands: 218 centimetres tall, a seated king in a blue robe with a five-clawed dragon on chest and shoulders. The original is kept in storage to slow its decay, and the museum in the compound shows portraits of later kings. Read the courtyard as administration instead. The stone stele by the gate told prince and peasant alike to get off their horse. And behind the halls stands a plain building worth more than any portrait: the Jeonju archive, one of the state's four libraries for the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty. When the Japanese invasion of 1592 burned the others, the shrine keeper and two local scholars carried this copy into a mountain cave and guarded it for about a year. Every surviving record of early Joseon runs through this courtyard.

Adults pay about ₩3,000. Winter hours are 09:00 to 18:00 with the last ticket at 17:00, and the last Wednesday of the month is free — but verify at the gate, because both move.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ₩3,000 for adults, ₩2,000 for teenagers and students, ₩1,000 for children; free for under-7s and over-65s and on the last Wednesday of the month. Prices and free-admission rules change — verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Winter (November to February) roughly 09:00 to 18:00, last admission 17:00; longer hours in summer. Open year-round. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level gravel and stone paths inside a walled compound, with one or two shallow steps at the inner gates. The main hall is viewed from outside, standing. Seating in the bamboo grove.
stops.insiderTip: The portrait faces the open doors of the main hall, so the doorframe makes a natural picture frame from the courtyard. Then walk past it to the archive building at the back — it looks like a storehouse, and it is the reason early Joseon's history still exists.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the main gate, cross to the stone wall and turn right along Taejo-ro, then take the first lane into the hanok quarter. Walk east uphill for about six hundred metres, keeping the tiled roofs on your right, until you reach the quiet stretch of Hyanggyo-gil where the old houses stand behind their gateposts.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bernard Gagnon, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Hanok Lanes & Hagindang
stops.narration:
Now walk the lanes. Hanok means simply "Korean house", but the word carries a whole construction system: a timber frame pegged and jointed rather than nailed, plaster and paper over wooden lattice, and a roof of dark curved tiles — giwa — laid on an earth-and-timber structure. The centre of the house is the madang, the open courtyard, which is the real living room in summer; the rooms wrap around it to block wind and keep the sun. Under the floor runs ondol, the traditional heating: a firebox outside the wall sends hot smoke along flues beneath heavy stone slabs, so the room is warm from below. It is the reason Koreans sit, eat and sleep on the floor.

Hagindang, on Hyanggyo-gil, is the oldest house in the village, built in 1908, and the only private home here carrying a heritage designation. It is run as a guesthouse now, so admire the gate, the deep eaves and the pond garden from the lane — do not walk in on somebody's breakfast.

And notice what these houses are not: ancient. In 1911 the colonial government pulled down Jeonju's city wall, Japanese shops took over the flat downtown, and Korean families — many of them comfortably off — answered by building tile-roofed houses on this slope. That is why the village looks like a Joseon film set while dating from the 1910s and 1930s. Of the 947 buildings here, 735 are hanok and 212 are not, and roughly 2,200 people live among the shops. Doors are doors, not exhibits. If the cold gets in, the Hanok Village History Museum is free and warm, and it explains how all of this happened.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Walking the lanes is free. Hagindang is a working guesthouse, not a museum, so it is not open for wandering; the local museums charge their own small fees.
stops.openingHours: Public lanes, open at all times. Shops, cafés and museums keep their own hours; several museums here close on Mondays.
stops.accessibility: Narrow lanes with cobbles, uneven paving and raised thresholds; most houses have a step or two up to a wooden porch. Fine on foot, difficult with wheels.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the low stone-and-tile walls: the top courses are set in decorative patterns that vary from house to house. Then find the village history museum, which is free and explains the colonial-era building boom in twenty warm minutes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Follow Hyanggyo-gil east and slightly uphill for about five hundred metres, past the last of the big walled houses, until the lane opens onto the stone steps and the long low school building above you on the right. That is the Confucian school.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Yun Ho Lee, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jeonju Hyanggyo (Confucian School)
stops.narration:
You are standing in the machinery of the Joseon state. A hyanggyo was a government-run provincial Confucian school: the place where local boys of the elite yangban class learned the Confucian classics and were drilled for the gwageo, the civil-service examinations that decided who governed the country. Confucianism here was less a religion of gods than a system for ordering families and a state — duty to parents, loyalty to the ruler, and above all jesa, the ancestor rites, performed on set days with food, wine and bows, which kept a lineage's dead present and its hierarchy real.

This school was founded in 1354 and has moved at least twice. It once stood on the ground where Gyeonggijeon was built, and settled on this hillside in 1603, after the Japanese invasions had wrecked the town. The hall behind you, Daeseongjeon, enshrines the spirit tablets of Confucius and other sages — seven Chinese scholars and eighteen Koreans. The long hall in front is where teaching happened. The ginkgo in the courtyard is about four hundred years old, so it has shaded roughly the whole life of this building.

Entry is free. Winter hours are 10:00 to 17:00, and it is closed Mondays; confirm at the gate, because small sites change their hours without warning.

Hold on to this place for the next twenty minutes. Ancestral rites were not private grief here; they were the constitutional order. Seven hundred metres downhill and west of here, in 1791, two Catholics refused to perform them — and the state killed them for it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry. Hours are short and the site closes one day a week, so confirm at the gate before you climb up.
stops.openingHours: Winter (November to February) 10:00 to 17:00; summer 09:00 to 18:00. Closed Mondays, and the following day when a Monday is a public holiday.
stops.accessibility: A short but genuine slope and a flight of stone steps up to the courtyard, then level packed earth and stone paving between the halls. No step-free route to the upper gate.
stops.insiderTip: Stand under the ginkgo and count the halls in a line — gate, lecture hall, courtyard, shrine hall. That single axis is how Confucian space arranges the world: learn outside, worship inside, dead at the far end.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down to the lane and turn right, then follow the path round the hillside for about six hundred metres to the stone staircase on your left. Climb it to the pavilion on top — that is Omokdae.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Steve46814, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Omokdae & Imokdae
stops.narration:
Climb to the pavilion and turn round. This is the shot: seven hundred-odd tiled roofs going blue-black in the cold, a wooded ridge behind, and not a glass tower in sight.

Omokdae is a low hill at the village's edge, and in September 1380 a general named Yi Seong-gye — twelve years before he became King Taejo — stopped here on his way home from breaking a Japanese pirate force that had been raiding the coast. His clan lived in Jeonju, so the town turned out for him, and he threw a banquet on this spot. At it he is said to have recited a poem about a great wind scattering the clouds and his need for warriors to defend the country. Everyone listening understood what that meant: a general announcing ambition. He took the throne in 1392.

What you are standing on is memory rather than evidence. The banquet is remembered as the moment the dynasty became thinkable, and the carved stone beside the pavilion is in the handwriting of Emperor Gojong, who reigned until 1907 and came here centuries later to mark the site.

A short walk from here stands Imokdae, where Yi Seong-gye's great-great-grandfather Yi An-sa lived before a quarrel with the Jeonju magistrate drove the family north. His descendants believed that quarrel put them on the road that ended in a crown. It is free and open at any hour, and it is genuinely steep — the staircase is stone, it ices over in December, and the handrail is there for a reason.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open at all hours, no ticket and no gate to verify — which is also why there is nobody to warn you about the ice.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in the low afternoon light; genuinely dangerous after snow or freezing rain.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: a steep flight of stone steps up a hillside to the pavilion, with more steps across the stream to Imokdae. The view is the reward, and it costs a climb.
stops.insiderTip: Come for the roofs, but look for the stele under its little shelter before you go — it carries the handwriting of Korea's last emperor, marking a spot that had become legend four centuries earlier.
stops.nextStopDirections: Descend the stairs on the far side of the hill and follow the lane downhill and west for about seven hundred metres, keeping the stream on your left. When the roofs open out and a red-brick spire appears ahead of you, you are standing in front of the cathedral.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 웬디러비, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Jeondong Catholic Cathedral
stops.narration:
Turn around and look at both sides of this street: the shrine of the dynasty's founder on one side, a Catholic cathedral on the other. The cathedral is here because this was an execution ground.

In the 1780s Catholicism reached Korea from China, and it spread first among scholars. The collision was over ancestral rites. For a Confucian state the ritual honouring of ancestors was the foundation of family and government; for a Catholic it was idolatry. In 1791 Yun Ji-chung refused the rites for his dead mother and burned the family's ancestral tablets. He and his cousin Kwon Sang-yeon were arrested and executed on this ground, which then lay just outside the south gate of the walled town — the first Korean Catholics to die for the faith. Ten years later, in the persecution of 1801, more were executed here, among them a man remembered as the Apostle of Honam. In 2014 Pope Francis declared Yun Ji-chung and 123 companions Blessed, one step short of sainthood.

The building itself came much later. A French priest bought the land in 1891; construction ran from 1908 to 1914 and the church was finally blessed in 1931. It was designed by Father Victor Louis Poisnel, the priest-architect who also worked on Myeongdong Cathedral in Seoul. Some of its bricks came from the town wall the colonial authorities had just demolished, and the cornerstone from a wall near the south gate — a church built out of the state that killed them. Romanesque below, Byzantine in its three domes.

Entry is free. It is a working church with daily Mass, so keep your voice down, and step outside if a service begins.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free. It is a working parish church, not a ticketed monument; donations go to upkeep, and tourists are asked to respect services.
stops.openingHours: Generally open to visitors during daylight hours, but closed around Mass times. Weekday Mass is early morning, with a late-morning Mass most weekdays; Sunday has several. Check the noticeboard at the door on the day.
stops.accessibility: Level entry from the street and a level nave. Ramps and step-free access depend on which door is open — ask at the parish office beside the church.
stops.insiderTip: Stand across the road and take in the pairing: state shrine on one side, martyrs' ground on the other. Then check the bricks at the base of the tower — some of them came out of the demolished city wall.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west from the cathedral for about two hundred metres, past the end of the hanok quarter, until you see the two-storey gatehouse standing alone in the middle of the road. Cross carefully at the lights: Pungnammun Gate is next.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jjw, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Pungnammun Gate
stops.narration:
One gate, and a city that is gone. Pungnammun was the south gate of Jeonju's walled town — the fortress that enclosed the provincial capital, with the governor's office inside the walls and this the ceremonial entrance, where each newly appointed governor was formally welcomed. The wall went up in the late Goryeo period, was wrecked in the Japanese invasion of 1597, was substantially rebuilt in 1734, and then a fire in 1767 took both the south and the west gates. The next year the governor rebuilt them and gave this one its name. It is Treasure No. 308, and the only one of the four gates still standing.

Why only one: in 1911, a year into colonial rule, the Japanese authorities levelled the city wall and left this gate alone. That single fact is why this walk exists. Once the wall was down, the land behind the gate was open, and Korean families built the hanok quarter right next to it.

The gate also marks where Jeonju's politics happened. In 1894 the Donghak peasant army took the city and forced the government into a truce and a reform programme. In March 1919, crowds gathered at the market just beyond the gate to shout for independence from Japan, and the city counts that as the start of its share in the movement. Free, open at all hours, floodlit after dark. It stands in the middle of a road, so watch the traffic rather than the history.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open access. The gatekeeper's pavilion upstairs is not normally open to visitors; ask at the small tourist office nearby.
stops.openingHours: Open at all times. Best after dark, when the gatehouse is lit and the market behind it is still working.
stops.accessibility: The gate stands on a level paved traffic island with kerbs and a controlled crossing. The wooden pavilion above the arch is reached only by a steep internal staircase.
stops.insiderTip: Walk round to the far side and look back through the arch towards the hanok rooftops — the gate frames the whole village, which is exactly how travellers arriving from the south saw Jeonju.
stops.nextStopDirections: Cross the road and walk straight through the gate into the covered market lanes behind it; the market runs for a couple of hundred metres. Head for the middle of the ground floor and then look for the staircase with the slogan painted on the wall.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Bcody80 at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Nambu Market & Youth Mall
stops.narration:
This is Jeonju's stomach, and it has been for a long time. The city claims markets on this ground since 1473; what is certain is that this one opened as a public market in 1905, outside the old south gate, and that by the late Joseon period it was counted among the country's three great markets — the rice floor of the Honam plain. Supermarkets hit it hard in the 1990s, shops emptied, and in 1999 a fire gutted the second floor of one building.

The revival came from above the ground floor. In 2011 the culture ministry turned that dead space into a Youth Mall: cheap rent, small units and a first shop for young traders who had never run one. Twenty-odd businesses now — a bookshop, a potter, a cocktail bar — under a slogan painted on the stairs: "earn moderately, live very well". Hours are roughly 11:00 to 23:00 and it shuts Mondays, so confirm at the door. The market's outdoor night market with food carts runs only on Friday and Saturday evenings; 29 and 30 December 2026 are a Tuesday and a Wednesday, so eat at the daytime kitchens instead.

Order the two dishes that made this city's name. Kongnamul-gukbap is a scalding bowl of bean-sprout soup with rice in it, invented as a hangover cure and eaten at any hour; a bowl runs around ₩8,000. Then bibimbap — Jeonju's version piles on soybean sprouts, yellow mung-bean jelly, beef and chilli paste. Nobody can prove it was born here, and the city lists several competing stories, but it was here that a rice-cake shop called Hankookjib started serving it in 1953 and made a market dish fit for a banquet.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk. Food is where the money goes: a bowl of bean-sprout soup around ₩8,000, a restaurant bibimbap around ₩12,000 to ₩15,000. Prices move — read the posted prices, and note that card payment is now common but cash is still preferred by some older stalls.
stops.openingHours: Ground-floor market roughly 04:00 to 18:00, and later on some stalls; the Youth Mall upstairs about 11:00 to 23:00, closed Mondays, with individual shops varying. The night market runs Fridays and Saturdays only, from about 18:00 to 23:30.
stops.accessibility: Level, covered market aisles, but narrow and busy with trolleys and crates. The Youth Mall is upstairs; ask a trader which of the staircases has the least steep flight.
stops.insiderTip: Go up to the Youth Mall's rooftop garden for a quiet view over the market roofs, then come down and eat at a ground-floor counter rather than a restaurant — the bean-sprout soup is the local breakfast, whatever the clock says.
stops.nextStopDirections: This is where the walking stops. The makgeolli houses are about three and a half kilometres south-west along busy roads — some forty-odd minutes on foot, and nobody strolls it in the cold and dark. Take a taxi (about ten minutes) or the city tour bus, which stops near the alley; if you do walk, keep to the main roads and give yourself an hour.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jjw, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Samcheon-dong Makgeolli Alley
stops.narration:
End here, in a lane of makgeolli houses. Makgeolli is Korea's oldest everyday drink: steamed rice mixed with nuruk, a starter cake of grain, mould and wild yeast, then left to ferment in a jar. It is never distilled and never filtered, so it pours milky, faintly fizzy and slightly sour-sweet, at around six or seven per cent alcohol. Filter it and you get cheongju, a clear rice wine; distil that and you get soju.

The drinking comes with a rule: pour for everyone else and never fill your own glass, hand the bottle over with two hands, and eat as you go. In Jeonju the eating is the point. Order one kettle here and the table fills — pancake, tofu, fish, a dozen small dishes — and order a second kettle and a different spread arrives. A kettle costs roughly ₩10,000 to ₩20,000, and set tables with food for two start around ₩40,000. The board in the window tells you where you stand, and it changes — so read it.

Why Jeonju has a lane like this: the city was once Korea's biggest makgeolli producer. Home brewing was criminalised under colonial liquor-tax laws, and from 1965 rice was banned from the mash for decades, so a generation grew up on thin wheat makgeolli. Rice came back at the end of the 1980s, home brewing only in 1995, and this alley grew up in the 1990s on that revival. It is about two hundred metres of Geomasan-ro with more than twenty houses, and the city now lists it as a piece of its future heritage.

Most houses open mid-afternoon and close around 22:00. If the cold has won, ask for moju — the same drink boiled with ginger, jujube and cinnamon, warmed and almost alcohol-free.
stops.entranceFeeNote: No entry fee. A kettle of makgeolli runs roughly ₩10,000 to ₩20,000 and set tables with side dishes start around ₩40,000 for two, with larger family tables well above that. Prices and opening hours vary house by house — check the board before you sit.
stops.openingHours: Individual houses, mostly from mid-afternoon until around 22:00 to 23:00, with last orders about an hour before closing. Some close one day a week. Check the notice on the door.
stops.accessibility: A level street of small ground-floor rooms. Traditional tables are low with floor cushions; most houses can seat you at a regular table if you ask at the door.
stops.insiderTip: Order by the kettle, not the bottle, and let the side dishes arrive before you order more — the second kettle usually brings a new spread, so a small group that drinks slowly eats far better than one that drinks fast.
stops.nextStopDirections: That is the end of the walk. You are three and a half kilometres south-west of the hanok quarter with a full table in front of you, so take a taxi back when you are ready — they queue on the main road at the end of the alley, and the ride is short. If you are staying in the village, the drivers all know the hanok quarter and the market; if you are staying on for New Year, the city rings the old bell at Pungnammun Gate on the last night of the year, which is as good a way as any to close out a day built on stone, soup and rice wine.
